```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(here)
library(broom)

here::i_am('seminars/week10-regression.qmd')

nhanes <- read_csv(here::here('data', 'mph_nhanes_20241107.csv'), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Recoding, verbatim from chapters/10-regression.qmd's own `recode` chunk
# (itself verbatim from Chapter 3): same levels, same labels, same order.
nhanes <- nhanes |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c('Male', 'Female')),
    eth = factor(eth,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c('Mexican American', 'Other Hispanic', 'White', 'Black', 'Others')),
    edu = factor(edu,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c('Less than high school', 'High school graduate', 'Above high school')),
    smoking = factor(smoking,
      levels = c('Never', 'Previous', 'Current')),
    phq.c = factor(phq.c,
      levels = c('0 Normal', '1 Mild symptoms', '2 Possible depression'),
      labels = c('Normal', 'Mild symptoms', 'Possible depression'),
      ordered = TRUE),
    blm.cvd = factor(blm.cvd,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c('No', 'Yes'))
  )

# Every quantity below is computed the same way chapters/10-regression.qmd
# computes it: same variable names, same steps, same function calls.

# Pearson: age and chol
age_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(chol))
ct_age <- cor.test(age_complete$age, age_complete$chol)

# Pearson: sed and chol
sed_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(sed), !is.na(chol))
ct_sed <- cor.test(sed_complete$sed, sed_complete$chol)

# Spearman: age and phq.c
phq_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(phq.c))
ct_spear <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(phq_complete$age, as.numeric(phq_complete$phq.c), method = 'spearman'))

# Simple linear regression: chol ~ age
m_age <- lm(chol ~ age, data = age_complete)
tidy_age <- tidy(m_age, conf.int = TRUE)
glance_age <- glance(m_age)
pred_age <- predict(m_age, newdata = data.frame(age = c(45, 150)), interval = 'confidence')
aug_age <- augment(m_age)
int_age <- tidy_age |> filter(term == '(Intercept)')
slope_age <- tidy_age |> filter(term == 'age')

# The age-model coefficient table, built once so the slope and intercept slides
# can re-show it without repeating the code (same values as 'How much does
# cholesterol differ per year of age?').
age_coef_gt <- tibble(
  Quantity = c('Intercept, cholesterol at age zero, mmol/L', 'Slope, per year of age, mmol/L'),
  Estimate = c(round(int_age$estimate, 3), round(slope_age$estimate, 5)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_age$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_age$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(slope_age$conf.low, 5), ' to ', round(slope_age$conf.high, 5))
  ),
  p = c('< 0.001', '< 0.001')
) |>
  gt()

# chol ~ gender, and the reconciliation with t.test()
gender_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(gender), !is.na(chol))
m_gender <- lm(chol ~ gender, data = gender_complete)
tidy_gender <- tidy(m_gender, conf.int = TRUE)
int_gender <- tidy_gender |> filter(term == '(Intercept)')
slope_gender <- tidy_gender |> filter(term == 'genderFemale')
tt_gender_eq <- t.test(chol ~ gender, data = gender_complete, var.equal = TRUE)

# chol ~ edu, and releveled
edu_complete <- nhanes |> filter(!is.na(edu), !is.na(chol))
m_edu <- lm(chol ~ edu, data = edu_complete)
tidy_edu <- tidy(m_edu, conf.int = TRUE)
glance_edu <- glance(m_edu)
int_edu <- tidy_edu |> filter(term == '(Intercept)')
hs_edu <- tidy_edu |> filter(term == 'eduHigh school graduate')
above_edu <- tidy_edu |> filter(term == 'eduAbove high school')

edu_relevelled <- edu_complete |> mutate(edu = relevel(edu, ref = 'Above high school'))
m_edu_relevel <- lm(chol ~ edu, data = edu_relevelled)
tidy_edu_relevel <- tidy(m_edu_relevel, conf.int = TRUE)
glance_edu_relevel <- glance(m_edu_relevel)

# sed carries a small number of physically implausible values (over 24
# hours/day), the same issue the Week 7 histogram met. The view is clipped
# with coord_cartesian(), never xlim() or a filter(), so bins aren't
# recomputed from a truncated dataset; the excluded count is said out loud
# on the slide that shows it.
sed_over24 <- sum(sed_complete$sed > 24, na.rm = TRUE)

# chol ~ sed, the closing synthesis for Block 2
m_sed <- lm(chol ~ sed, data = sed_complete)
tidy_sed <- tidy(m_sed, conf.int = TRUE)
glance_sed <- glance(m_sed)
slope_sed <- tidy_sed |> filter(term == 'sed')

# Gentamicin clearance in babies, a retained teaching example per the
# narrow exception to the worked-example rule (shared-ground-rules.md,
# settled 2026-09-28): neither nhanes_mph nor strep_tb can produce an
# impossible prediction the way this one does. Numbers retyped from the
# source deck's own Stata output, not recomputed (the raw data was never
# digitised): slides_2025/Correlation and Regression AMcI 20251114.pptx,
# slides 26, 27, 36 and 37. n = 31 babies, clearance (l/h) regressed on
# weight (kg). Lightest baby about 0.9 kg, read off the source deck's slide 25
# scatterplot (image only, no data table), for the 300 g slide.
# The gentamicin slide's markdown table retypes the intercept, slope, CIs and
# p-values below by hand (no value on it is computed): keep the two in step.
gent_n <- 31
gent_intercept <- -0.027
gent_intercept_ci <- c(-0.047, -0.008)
gent_slope <- 0.074
gent_slope_ci <- c(0.066, 0.082)
gent_r2 <- 0.926
gent_pred_3kg <- round(gent_intercept + gent_slope * 3, 3)
gent_pred_300g <- round(gent_intercept + gent_slope * 0.3, 3)

# Application: Potter GDM, Cade JE, Hardie LJ. 'Longer sleep is associated
# with lower BMI and favorable metabolic profiles in UK adults: findings
# from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey.' PLOS ONE 2017;12(7):e0182195,
# https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0182195. CC BY 4.0, so retyping this
# small an extract is unambiguously fine to publish. Verified against the
# published Table 3 and its surrounding text. The model is adjusted for age,
# ethnicity, sex, smoking, and socioeconomic status.
# The Application slide's markdown table retypes app_estimate and app_ci: keep in step.
app_n <- 1615
app_estimate <- -0.46
app_ci <- c(-0.69, -0.24)
```

## What you have learnt so far

- **Stats, Week 9.** We learnt t-tests for comparing a continuous variable between groups, and the chi-squared test for two categorical variables. But what if we want to examine the association between two continuous variables, e.g., cholesterol and age?
- **Epi, Week 1.** Exposure and outcome as hypothetical causes and the health state of interest. How can we model them statistically?
- **Epi, Week 4.** Correlation is not causation was mentioned but what exactly is 'correlation'?

## By the end of this week, you will be able to

1. Select an appropriate correlation measure and interpret the findings
2. Apply the simple linear regression model, and assess its assumptions using residual diagnostics
3. Interpret the intercept and slope with confidence intervals and p-values
4. Use a fitted model for prediction, and explain the danger of extrapolation

## Block 1: correlation {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## There are no two groups here

- We can compare two groups. Last week's exposure was gender, a two-category label
- This week's exposures are age and sedentary time, both are continuous[]{.gap}
- We can't apply a t-test with these as exposure
- But the question is still the same one we've been asking all term: does the outcome differ, and by how much, as the exposure changes

## Visualising two continuous variables at once {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Boxplot and histogram to examine distribution of a continuous variable by groups
- Scatterplot is for two continuous variables
- One point per participant, one variable on each axis[]{.gap}
- The cloud slopes gently upward and is wide
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: scatter-age
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
ggplot(age_complete, aes(x = age, y = chol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(x = 'Age (years)', y = 'Total cholesterol (mmol/L)')
```

:::
::::

## Pearson's correlation coefficient, r {.smaller}

- The scatterplot seems to follow a straight line going upward. But it is too noisy to be sure
- Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength of a straight-line association between two continuous variables
- Its range is minus 1 to plus 1, with 0 meaning no linear association. The null value for a test on r is 0
- Neither variable is treated as the outcome: r is symmetric[]{.gap}
- r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / √[Σ(x − x̄)² · Σ(y − ȳ)²]
  - Each variable enters only through its own distance from its own mean, divided by its own spread
  - That's why r carries no units

## Age and cholesterol: what is r? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: cor-age-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = 'Pearson r, age and total cholesterol',
  Estimate = round(unname(ct_age$estimate), 3),
  `95% CI` = paste0(round(ct_age$conf.int[1], 3), ' to ', round(ct_age$conf.int[2], 3)),
  p = if (ct_age$p.value < 0.001) '< 0.001' else as.character(round(ct_age$p.value, 3))
) |>
  gt()
```

- H0: r is 0, i.e., no linear association between age and cholesterol
- H1: r is not 0[]{.gap}
- Age and total cholesterol were positively correlated (r = `r round(unname(ct_age$estimate), 3)`, 95% CI `r round(ct_age$conf.int[1], 3)` to `r round(ct_age$conf.int[2], 3)`, p `r if (ct_age$p.value < 0.001) '< 0.001' else paste('=', round(ct_age$p.value, 3))`)
- The association is non-zero but weak, matching the wide, gently sloping cloud in the scatterplot

## What different values of r look like

```{r}
#| label: r-gallery
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.6
set.seed(1)
n_gal <- 200
gallery_r <- c(0.9, 0.5, 0, -0.5, -0.9)
gallery_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gallery_r, function(r) {
  z1 <- rnorm(n_gal)
  z2 <- rnorm(n_gal)
  x <- z1
  y <- r * z1 + sqrt(1 - r^2) * z2
  data.frame(r = paste0('r = ', r), x = x, y = y)
}))
gallery_df$r <- factor(gallery_df$r, levels = paste0('r = ', gallery_r))

ggplot(gallery_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ r, nrow = 1) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## r does not depend on the units {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Same participants, same cholesterol: only the unit of age changes
- r is identical for age in years and age in months[]{.gap}
- This is why r often can be compared across studies
- But also why r can't answer 'how much cholesterol changes per year of age'
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: r-units
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
units_df <- bind_rows(
  age_complete |> transmute(x = age, chol, panel = paste0('Age in years, r = ', round(cor(age, chol), 3))),
  age_complete |> transmute(x = age * 12, chol, panel = paste0('Age in months, r = ', round(cor(age * 12, chol), 3)))
)
units_df$panel <- factor(units_df$panel, levels = unique(units_df$panel))

ggplot(units_df, aes(x = x, y = chol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.03) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = 'free_x') +
  labs(x = 'Age', y = 'Total cholesterol (mmol/L)')
```

:::
::::

## When r misleads

```{r}
#| label: r-misleads
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
set.seed(2)
n_mis <- 150

curved_x <- runif(n_mis, -3, 3)
curved_y <- -(curved_x^2) + rnorm(n_mis, sd = 1.2)
panel1 <- data.frame(panel = 'A real curve, r near zero', x = curved_x, y = curved_y)

out_x <- c(rnorm(n_mis - 1, 0, 1), 8)
out_y <- c(rnorm(n_mis - 1, 0, 1), 8)
panel2 <- data.frame(panel = 'One outlier, changing r', x = out_x, y = out_y)

full_x <- rnorm(n_mis, 0, 3)
full_y <- 0.7 * full_x + rnorm(n_mis, sd = 1)
restrict_df <- data.frame(x = full_x, y = full_y)
restrict_df <- restrict_df[abs(restrict_df$x) < 0.6, ]
panel3 <- data.frame(panel = 'A restricted range, flattened', x = restrict_df$x, y = restrict_df$y)

sub1_x <- rnorm(n_mis / 2, 0, 1); sub1_y <- 0.8 * sub1_x + rnorm(n_mis / 2, sd = 0.5) + 4
sub2_x <- rnorm(n_mis / 2, 4, 1); sub2_y <- 0.8 * sub2_x + rnorm(n_mis / 2, sd = 0.5) - 4
panel4 <- data.frame(panel = 'Two subgroups, opposite pull', x = c(sub1_x, sub2_x), y = c(sub1_y, sub2_y))

misleads_df <- bind_rows(panel1, panel2, panel3, panel4)
misleads_df$panel <- factor(misleads_df$panel, levels = c(
  'A real curve, r near zero', 'One outlier, changing r',
  'A restricted range, flattened', 'Two subgroups, opposite pull'
))

ggplot(misleads_df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = 'free') +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

- Four ways a linear coefficient hides or invents a relationship
- All four can be identified from a scatterplot, which is why we always plot the data first

## This week's methodological anchor {.smaller}

- [Bland and Altman (1994)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8019296/), *BMJ*: 'Correlation, regression, and repeated data'
- Their worked case: five subjects, each measured five times
  - Taking the mean of each subject before calculating the correlation gives r of -0.67 (p = 0.22)
  - Pooling all 25 data points before calculating the correlation gives r of -0.47 (p = 0.02)[]{.gap}
- Pooling manufactured a significant result out of data that didn't have one
- This is the independence assumption behind every test in this course
- The paired t-test meets it by analysing one difference per person

## Correlation for ordinal variables {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}

- Pearson's r assumes both variables sit on a scale where equal steps mean the same thing throughout
  - For age, the difference between 30 and 29 is the same as that between 60 and 59: 1 year
- An ordinal variable doesn't: the step from 'no symptoms' to 'mild symptoms' isn't the same size as the step from 'mild symptoms' to 'possible depression'[]{.gap}
- Spearman's rho is Pearson's r computed on the ranks of the observations instead of their raw values
  - It needs the observations put in order
  - It also handles a relationship that's consistently increasing or decreasing without being a straight line
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}

```{r}
#| label: spearman-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
set.seed(4)
rank_x <- runif(80, 0, 4)
rank_y <- exp(rank_x) + rnorm(80, sd = 3)
rank_r <- cor(rank_x, rank_y)
rank_rho <- cor(rank_x, rank_y, method = 'spearman')

ggplot(data.frame(x = rank_x, y = rank_y), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    title = paste0('Pearson r = ', round(rank_r, 2), '; Spearman rho = ', round(rank_rho, 2))
  ) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

:::
::::

## Is age associated with depression symptom category?

```{r}
#| label: spearman-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = 'Age and depression symptom category, Spearman rho',
  Estimate = round(unname(ct_spear$estimate), 3),
  `95% CI` = 'not available',
  p = format(round(ct_spear$p.value, 2), nsmall = 2)
) |>
  gt()
```

- Rho is close to zero, and the p-value is far from significant: no clear ordered relationship in this sample
- No CI accompanies it. Rho has no simple formula for one[]{.gap}

## Try it: Pearson or Spearman?

| Pair | Variable 1 | Variable 2 |
|--|----------|----------|
| A | Age (years) | Total cholesterol (mmol/L) |
| B | Sedentary time (hours/day) | Total cholesterol (mmol/L) |
| C | Age group (20-30, 31-40, 41-50) | Depression score, PHQ-2 (0 to 6) |
| D | Education (less than high school, high school graduate, above high school) | Depression symptom category |

- For each pair, would we report Pearson's r or Spearman's rho?
- What in the variables decides it?
- Three minutes

## Try it: the answer

| Pair | Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Measure |
|--|----------|----------|-----|
| A | Age (years) | Total cholesterol (mmol/L) | Pearson's r |
| B | Sedentary time (hours/day) | Total cholesterol (mmol/L) | Pearson's r |
| C | Age group (20-30, 31-40, 41-50) | Depression score, PHQ-2 (0 to 6) | Spearman's rho |
| D | Education (less than high school, high school graduate, above high school) | Depression symptom category | Spearman's rho |

- Pair A and pair B still need a scatterplot first, since r only measures a straight-line association

## What a correlation cannot tell us

- The coefficient for age and cholesterol was `r round(unname(ct_age$estimate), 3)`
- It says the two move together weakly, but doesn't say:
  - whether age is the cause or the other way round (an epi question)
  - how much cholesterol differs between a 40 year old and a 60 year old (a stats question)[]{.gap}

## Block 2: simple linear regression and diagnostics {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## The response and the explanatory variable

- When we are asking questions like 'how much cholesterol differs between a 40 year old and a 60 year old', we are often making implicit assumptions about what we want to explain:
  - Cholesterol is the **response**, the variable being explained
  - Age is the **explanatory variable**, the one doing the explaining[]{.gap}
- Mapping the terminology from epi: the outcome is the response, the exposure is the explanatory variable

## Try it: name the response

| Study | Question |
|--|------------|
| 1 | Does blood pressure vary by daily salt intake? |
| 2 | Would hours of revision affect exam score? |
| 3 | Is cigarettes smoked per day in pregnancy a risk factor for birth weight? |
| 4 | Does cholesterol become higher with older age? |

- For each study, which variable is the response, and what in the question decides it?
- Three minutes

## Try it: the answer {.smaller}

| Study | Question | Response | Explanatory variable |
|--|------------|-----|-----|
| 1 | Does blood pressure vary by daily salt intake? | Blood pressure | Daily salt intake |
| 2 | Would hours of revision affect exam score? | Exam score | Hours of revision |
| 3 | Is cigarettes smoked per day in pregnancy a risk factor for birth weight? | Birth weight | Cigarettes smoked per day |
| 4 | Does cholesterol become higher with older age? | Cholesterol | Age |

- The response is the variable the question wants explained[]{.gap}
- The explanatory variable is the one that could plausibly have come first
- Study 4: age cannot depend on cholesterol, so age has to be the explanatory variable
- The software would fit it either way round: the direction comes from the question, not the arithmetic

## A regression model to answer these questions {.smaller}

- All these questions can be answered using a simple linear regression:
- Y = α + βX + ε
  - Y: the response
  - α: the intercept
  - β: the slope
  - X: the explanatory variable
  - ε: the error the line doesn't capture[]{.gap}
- X and Y are observed (the data)
- α and β are model **coefficients** to be estimated

## Fitting the line: least squares {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}

- Ideally we want to estimate α and β so that the error is minimised
- We can't because error is unobserved. We don't know the population regression line.
- Instead we target the next best thing: the **residual**, the *vertical* distance between the estimated regression line and the data
- Least squares picks the one line that makes the sum of the squared residuals smallest[]{.gap}
- Vertical, not horizontal: the line is fitted to explain the response (vertical axis), so it's the response's own errors that get minimised
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}

```{r}
#| label: least-squares-schematic
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.6
set.seed(3)
ls_demo_x <- 1:10
ls_demo_y <- 2 + 0.8 * ls_demo_x + rnorm(10, sd = 1.3)
ls_demo_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data.frame(x = ls_demo_x, y = ls_demo_y))
ls_demo_bad_b0 <- 1
ls_demo_bad_b1 <- 0.3

bad_df <- data.frame(panel = 'A badly fitted line', x = ls_demo_x, y = ls_demo_y)
bad_df$fit <- ls_demo_bad_b0 + ls_demo_bad_b1 * bad_df$x
bad_df$b0 <- ls_demo_bad_b0
bad_df$b1 <- ls_demo_bad_b1

good_df <- data.frame(panel = 'The least-squares line', x = ls_demo_x, y = ls_demo_y)
good_df$fit <- predict(ls_demo_fit)
good_df$b0 <- coef(ls_demo_fit)[1]
good_df$b1 <- coef(ls_demo_fit)[2]

demo_df <- bind_rows(bad_df, good_df)
demo_df$panel <- factor(demo_df$panel, levels = c('A badly fitted line', 'The least-squares line'))
abline_df <- demo_df |> distinct(panel, b0, b1)

ggplot(demo_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = fit), color = '#C0392B', linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(data = abline_df, aes(intercept = b0, slope = b1), color = '#4386AF', linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

:::
::::

## Finding the line by hand {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: ls-widget
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
set.seed(42)
ls_x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4.5, 5.5, 6, 7, 8, 9)
ls_y <- round(2 + 0.9 * ls_x + rnorm(10, sd = 1.1), 2)
ls_fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data.frame(x = ls_x, y = ls_y))
ls_best_b0 <- round(unname(coef(ls_fit)[1]), 2)
ls_best_b1 <- round(unname(coef(ls_fit)[2]), 2)
ls_best_ss <- round(sum(residuals(ls_fit)^2), 2)
ls_pts_json <- paste0('[', paste(sprintf('[%.2f,%.2f]', ls_x, ls_y), collapse = ','), ']')

cat(sprintf('
<div id="ls-widget" style="text-align:center;">
<div style="margin-bottom:0.3em;">
<label style="font-size:0.85em;">Intercept
<input type="range" id="ls-intercept" min="0" max="6" step="0.5" value="3" style="vertical-align:middle;">
</label>
<label style="font-size:0.85em;margin-left:1em;">Slope
<input type="range" id="ls-slope" min="-0.5" max="2" step="0.1" value="0.3" style="vertical-align:middle;">
</label>
</div>
<svg id="ls-svg" width="760" height="330" style="max-width:100%%;"></svg>
<div>
<button id="ls-show-best" style="font-size:0.8em;padding:0.25em 0.7em;margin:0.15em;background:#00213B;color:#fff;border:none;border-radius:4px;cursor:pointer;">Show least-squares line</button>
<button id="ls-reset" style="font-size:0.8em;padding:0.25em 0.7em;margin:0.15em;background:#ABB5C5;color:#00213B;border:none;border-radius:4px;cursor:pointer;">Reset</button>
</div>
<div id="ls-caption" style="margin-top:0.3em;font-size:0.9em;"></div>
</div>
<script>
(function() {
  var pts = %s;
  var bestB0 = %s, bestB1 = %s, bestSS = %s;
  var svg = document.getElementById("ls-svg");
  var ns = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  var w = 760, h = 330;
  var marginTop = 16, marginRight = 16, marginBottom = 34, marginLeft = 44;
  var plotW = w - marginLeft - marginRight;
  var plotH = h - marginTop - marginBottom;
  var xMin = 0, xMax = 10, yMin = 0, yMax = 16;
  var showBest = false;

  function xPix(x) { return marginLeft + (x - xMin) / (xMax - xMin) * plotW; }
  function yPix(y) { return marginTop + (1 - (y - yMin) / (yMax - yMin)) * plotH; }

  function sumSquares(b0, b1) {
    var ss = 0;
    pts.forEach(function(p) {
      var resid = p[1] - (b0 + b1 * p[0]);
      ss += resid * resid;
    });
    return ss;
  }

  function draw() {
    while (svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    var xAxis = document.createElementNS(ns, "line");
    xAxis.setAttribute("x1", xPix(xMin)); xAxis.setAttribute("y1", yPix(yMin));
    xAxis.setAttribute("x2", xPix(xMax)); xAxis.setAttribute("y2", yPix(yMin));
    xAxis.setAttribute("stroke", "#00213B");
    svg.appendChild(xAxis);
    var yAxis = document.createElementNS(ns, "line");
    yAxis.setAttribute("x1", xPix(xMin)); yAxis.setAttribute("y1", yPix(yMin));
    yAxis.setAttribute("x2", xPix(xMin)); yAxis.setAttribute("y2", yPix(yMax));
    yAxis.setAttribute("stroke", "#00213B");
    svg.appendChild(yAxis);

    var b0 = parseFloat(document.getElementById("ls-intercept").value);
    var b1 = parseFloat(document.getElementById("ls-slope").value);

    pts.forEach(function(p) {
      var fitted = b0 + b1 * p[0];
      var seg = document.createElementNS(ns, "line");
      seg.setAttribute("x1", xPix(p[0])); seg.setAttribute("y1", yPix(p[1]));
      seg.setAttribute("x2", xPix(p[0])); seg.setAttribute("y2", yPix(fitted));
      seg.setAttribute("stroke", "#C0392B");
      seg.setAttribute("stroke-dasharray", "3,3");
      svg.appendChild(seg);
    });

    var line = document.createElementNS(ns, "line");
    line.setAttribute("x1", xPix(xMin)); line.setAttribute("y1", yPix(b0 + b1 * xMin));
    line.setAttribute("x2", xPix(xMax)); line.setAttribute("y2", yPix(b0 + b1 * xMax));
    line.setAttribute("stroke", "#4386AF");
    line.setAttribute("stroke-width", "2.5");
    svg.appendChild(line);

    if (showBest) {
      var bline = document.createElementNS(ns, "line");
      bline.setAttribute("x1", xPix(xMin)); bline.setAttribute("y1", yPix(bestB0 + bestB1 * xMin));
      bline.setAttribute("x2", xPix(xMax)); bline.setAttribute("y2", yPix(bestB0 + bestB1 * xMax));
      bline.setAttribute("stroke", "#1B7A3D");
      bline.setAttribute("stroke-width", "2.5");
      bline.setAttribute("stroke-dasharray", "6,3");
      svg.appendChild(bline);
    }

    pts.forEach(function(p) {
      var c = document.createElementNS(ns, "circle");
      c.setAttribute("cx", xPix(p[0])); c.setAttribute("cy", yPix(p[1]));
      c.setAttribute("r", 5);
      c.setAttribute("fill", "#00213B");
      svg.appendChild(c);
    });

    var ss = sumSquares(b0, b1);
    var caption = "Your line: intercept " + b0.toFixed(1) + ", slope " + b1.toFixed(1) +
      ". Sum of squared residuals: " + ss.toFixed(1);
    if (showBest) {
      caption += ". Least-squares line: intercept " + bestB0.toFixed(2) + ", slope " + bestB1.toFixed(2) +
        ", sum of squared residuals " + bestSS.toFixed(1) + " (the smallest possible)";
    }
    document.getElementById("ls-caption").textContent = caption;
  }

  ["ls-intercept", "ls-slope"].forEach(function(id) {
    var el = document.getElementById(id);
    el.addEventListener("input", draw);
    el.addEventListener("keydown", function(e) { e.stopPropagation(); });
  });

  document.getElementById("ls-show-best").addEventListener("click", function() {
    showBest = true;
    draw();
  });
  document.getElementById("ls-reset").addEventListener("click", function() {
    showBest = false;
    document.getElementById("ls-intercept").value = 3;
    document.getElementById("ls-slope").value = 0.3;
    draw();
  });

  draw();
})();
</script>
', ls_pts_json, ls_best_b0, ls_best_b1, ls_best_ss))
```

- Drag the sliders to change the line, and watch the sum of squared residuals rise and fall
- Every line has a total squared error, and exactly one line makes it smallest[]{.gap}

## How much does cholesterol differ per year of age? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-age-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c('Intercept, cholesterol at age zero, mmol/L', 'Slope, per year of age, mmol/L'),
  Estimate = c(round(int_age$estimate, 3), round(slope_age$estimate, 5)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_age$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_age$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(slope_age$conf.low, 5), ' to ', round(slope_age$conf.high, 5))
  ),
  p = c('< 0.001', '< 0.001')
) |>
  gt()
```

- Let's focus on the slope first, because it shows whether, and to which extent, cholesterol changes with age:
- H0: the slope of cholesterol on age is zero, i.e., cholesterol doesn't vary with age
- H1: the slope is not zero, i.e., cholesterol varies with age[]{.gap}
- Total cholesterol was on average `r round(slope_age$estimate, 4)` mmol/L higher for each additional year of age (95% CI `r round(slope_age$conf.low, 4)` to `r round(slope_age$conf.high, 4)` mmol/L, p < 0.001)

## Reading the slope {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: age-coef-slope
#| echo: false
age_coef_gt
```

- The slope is the difference in mean cholesterol associated with one additional year of age, in mmol/L per year
- Across the twenty years between 40 and 60 that's about `r round(slope_age$estimate * 20, 2)` mmol/L, the answer a correlation coefficient could never give[]{.gap}
- We say 'associated with', not 'causes' because we can't be sure it is causal

## Reading the intercept {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: age-coef-intercept
#| echo: false
age_coef_gt
```

- The intercept is the model's fitted value where the explanatory variable is zero: here, `r round(int_age$estimate, 2)` mmol/L at age zero
- Nobody in this survey is a newborn, so this intercept is a mathematical anchor that minimises the residuals, not something we want to interpret[]{.gap}
- The intercept becomes a real, interpretable number as soon as the explanatory variable is a set of categories, coming up shortly

## The fitted line on the data {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- The least-squares line for cholesterol on age, drawn over the scatterplot from Block 1
- The shaded band is a 95% CI for the line, drawn as a band instead of two numbers[]{.gap}
- The band is narrow because n is large
- The points still scatter widely around it indicating age per se doesn't explain much of the variation in cholesterol
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: scatter-age-line
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
ggplot(age_complete, aes(x = age, y = chol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm') +
  labs(x = 'Age (years)', y = 'Total cholesterol (mmol/L)')
```

## The full output {.full-output}

```{r}
#| label: summary-age
#| echo: false
options(width = 76)
summary(m_age)
```

- R prints all of this at once. The coefficient tables on earlier slides are taken from this printout

## What else the output carries {.smaller}

- Three quantities sit alongside the coefficients, in the last lines of the printout (R squared has its own slide next):

```{r}
#| label: summary-age-tail
#| echo: false
options(width = 76)
out_lines <- capture.output(summary(m_age))
cat(tail(out_lines[nzchar(out_lines)], 3), sep = '\n')
```

- The **residual standard error**: the typical size of a residual, in the response's units. Here, `r round(glance_age$sigma, 2)` mmol/L. It describes how far the points sit from the line, not how precise the line is
- The **F-statistic** tests the model as a whole. With one explanatory variable, that's the same question the slope's own test already answers. It is more useful when we have more explanatory variables in the model[]{.gap}

## Multiple R-squared {.smaller}

- **Multiple R-squared** is the proportion of the response's total variation the model accounts for, from 0 to 1
- R² = 1 − (residual sum of squares / total sum of squares)[]{.gap}
- With one explanatory variable, R squared is exactly the square of Pearson's r, and hence the name
- We report it because it answers a different question from the slope's p-value: not whether the association is real, but how much of the response the model explains

## Cholesterol and age: R squared is under 1%

- R squared is `r round(glance_age$r.squared, 4)`: age accounts for under 1% of the variation in cholesterol between participants[]{.gap}
- Set that against the slope's p-value, well below 0.001, on the same model
- An association can be real, precisely estimated, and still leave almost all of the response unexplained

## Can we trust the regression line?

- Fitting the regression line is very easy (you can do it in Excel), but interpreting it and judging whether it's reliable is harder
- It would still fit if the relationship were curved, if the scatter widened as age rose, or if the same people had been measured several times[]{.gap}
- Nothing in the output distinguishes those cases from a well-behaved one, so the check has to be made deliberately

## What the model assumes

- **Linearity**: a straight line is the right shape
- **Constant variance**: the scatter doesn't widen along the line
- **Normally distributed errors**: we don't know the true errors but can look at the residuals[]{.gap}
- **Independence between observations**: a property of how the data were collected, not something we can show from a plot or a test

## Residuals against fitted values

- Plotting each residual against its fitted value checks linearity and constant variance together
- An even band around zero, with no curve and no change in spread from left to right, is what a well-behaved model looks like[]{.gap}

## Cholesterol and age: residuals against fitted {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- Most points sit in an even band around zero
  - There's no visible trend
  - The spread also looks constant along the fitted line
- A small group of participants with very high cholesterol sit well above it
  - They can be genuine outliers, e.g., someone whose disease puts them well outside the population norm
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: resid-fitted-age
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(aug_age, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = 'Fitted value (mmol/L)', y = 'Residual (mmol/L)')
```

:::
::::

## The QQ plot

- The standardised residuals, plotted against what a normal distribution would have produced, with a reference line
- Points on the line are consistent with normally distributed residuals

## Cholesterol and age: the QQ plot {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}

- The middle of the distribution sits close to the line. The upper tail pulls away: the same high-cholesterol participants again
- With `r format(nobs(m_age), big.mark = ',')` participants, the estimates hold up despite it because of the CLT. In a small sample, this same picture would be a real concern[]{.gap}
- Taken together, the checks suggest the findings are reasonably reliable
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}

```{r}
#| label: qq-age
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(aug_age, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(x = 'Theoretical quantiles', y = 'Standardised residuals')
```

## Block 3: a categorical explanatory variable {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## When the explanatory variable has categories {.smaller}

- A simple linear regression describes how a continuous response varies with a continuous explanatory variable
- What if the explanatory variable is categorical?
- The simplest case: a binary variable
  - Same as the coin flip example, we will need to convert the categories to 0 and 1:
  - The 'reference category' (the category to compare with) becomes 0
  - The 'active category' becomes 1
- The intercept becomes the mean of the reference[]{.gap}
- The slope becomes the difference of active minus reference

## Does cholesterol differ between men and women?

```{r}
#| label: lm-gender-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c('Intercept, mean cholesterol in men, mmol/L', 'Slope for women, mmol/L'),
  Estimate = c(round(int_gender$estimate, 3), round(slope_gender$estimate, 3)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_gender$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_gender$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(slope_gender$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(slope_gender$conf.high, 3))
  ),
  p = c('< 0.001', '< 0.001')
) |>
  gt()
```

- H0: mean total cholesterol is the same in men and women
- H1: it differs[]{.gap}
- Mean total cholesterol was `r round(slope_gender$estimate, 2)` mmol/L higher in women than in men (95% CI `r round(slope_gender$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(slope_gender$conf.high, 2)` mmol/L, p < 0.001)

## This is a replication of the t-test

- Week 9 reported this exact comparison: `r round(slope_gender$estimate, 2)` mmol/L higher in women, 95% CI `r round(slope_gender$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(slope_gender$conf.high, 2)` mmol/L
- The two agree to several decimal places here, because the two groups happen to have nearly the same spread[]{.gap}
- The two procedures aren't identical, though: a t-test's default doesn't assume the groups share a spread, and a regression does
- In practice the two answers rarely differ materially

## When the explanatory variable has three categories {.smaller}

- A regression model also handles an explanatory variable with more than two categories
- Say for a three-category variable:
  - The 'reference category' (the category to compare with) is 0 on every indicator
  - The first 'active category' gets a 0/1 indicator (also known as *dummy variable*)
  - Each further 'active category' gets its own 0/1 indicator
- All comparisons are made against the reference[]{.gap}

## Does cholesterol differ by education? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-edu-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "Intercept, mean cholesterol, 'less than high school', mmol/L",
    "Slope for 'High school graduate', mmol/L",
    "Slope for 'Above high school', mmol/L"
  ),
  Estimate = c(round(int_edu$estimate, 3), round(hs_edu$estimate, 3), round(above_edu$estimate, 3)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(hs_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(hs_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(above_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(above_edu$conf.high, 3))
  ),
  p = c('n/a', format(round(hs_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3), format(round(above_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3))
) |>
  gt()
```

- H0: a non-reference category's mean cholesterol equals the reference category's
- H1: it differs[]{.gap}
- 'High school graduate' against 'less than high school': a difference in mean cholesterol of `r round(hs_edu$estimate, 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r round(hs_edu$conf.low, 3)` to `r round(hs_edu$conf.high, 3)` mmol/L, p = `r format(round(hs_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3)`)
- 'Above high school' against 'less than high school': `r round(above_edu$estimate, 3)` mmol/L (95% CI `r round(above_edu$conf.low, 3)` to `r round(above_edu$conf.high, 3)` mmol/L, p = `r format(round(above_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3)`)[]{.gap}
- Both 95% CIs include zero: these data show no clear association between education and cholesterol

## Changing the reference

- A reference category is arbitrary and decided based on the research question and framing
- It changes the numbers because the comparison changes, but the fit stays the same
- R squared (`r format(glance_edu$r.squared, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)`, both parameterisations) and the residual standard error don't move at all[]{.gap}

## Try it: read the education table {.smaller}

#| echo: false

  ),
  Estimate = c(round(int_edu$estimate, 3), round(hs_edu$estimate, 3), round(above_edu$estimate, 3)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(hs_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(hs_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(above_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(above_edu$conf.high, 3))
  ),

- Which education category is the reference, and how can you tell from the table alone?
- What's the model's estimated mean cholesterol for a participant in each of the three categories?[]{.gap}
- What would happen to the coefficients, and to R squared, if 'above high school' were made the reference instead?
- Three minutes

## Try it: the answer {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: answer-edu-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "Intercept, mean cholesterol, 'less than high school', mmol/L",
    "Slope for 'High school graduate', mmol/L",
    "Slope for 'Above high school', mmol/L"
  ),
  Estimate = c(round(int_edu$estimate, 3), round(hs_edu$estimate, 3), round(above_edu$estimate, 3)),
  `95% CI` = c(
    paste0(round(int_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(int_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(hs_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(hs_edu$conf.high, 3)),
    paste0(round(above_edu$conf.low, 3), ' to ', round(above_edu$conf.high, 3))
  ),
  p = c('n/a', format(round(hs_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3), format(round(above_edu$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3))
) |>
  gt()
```

- The reference is the one category without a row of its own: 'less than high school', mean `r round(int_edu$estimate, 3)` mmol/L[]{.gap}
- The other two are the intercept plus their own contrasts: `r round(int_edu$estimate + hs_edu$estimate, 3)` mmol/L and `r round(int_edu$estimate + above_edu$estimate, 3)` mmol/L
- The rows would become contrasts against 'above high school', while R squared stayed the same, because the fit is the same fit

## Block 4: prediction {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## Using the model to predict {.smaller}

- 'Predict' is used loosely here. We are not predicting what would happen in the future
- Instead, we are *interpolating* or *extrapolating*
- Consider a toy example with 3 data points: cholesterol readings from people aged 30, 50, and 70
  - Interpolation is to use the regression model to estimate the average cholesterol for 31, 40, and 60 year olds even if our data don't include these exact ages
  - Extrapolation is to use the regression model to estimate the average cholesterol for 29 and 75 year olds

## Confidence and prediction intervals {.smaller}

- Put a value of the explanatory variable into the fitted regression line, and it returns a fitted value for the response, with a CI round it
- That CI describes the precision of the predicted **mean**, not of a single **individual**[]{.gap}
- A **prediction interval**, a different quantity from a CI, describes the precision for an individual. It's always wider, since predicting one person is less certain than predicting the average across many
- In public health we mostly report the CI, not the prediction interval
- A prediction interval could in theory be useful in precision medicine, but it is usually too wide to be useful

## Predicted mean cholesterol at age 45

- The fitted regression line: cholesterol = α + β × age[]{.gap}
- Substituting the estimates: `r round(int_age$estimate, 3)` + `r round(slope_age$estimate, 5)` × 45
  - The slope term: `r round(slope_age$estimate, 5)` × 45 = `r round(slope_age$estimate * 45, 2)`
  - Adding the intercept: `r round(int_age$estimate, 3)` + `r round(slope_age$estimate * 45, 2)` = `r round(int_age$estimate + slope_age$estimate * 45, 2)` mmol/L
- With a 95% CI of `r round(pred_age[1, 'lwr'], 2)` to `r round(pred_age[1, 'upr'], 2)` mmol/L[]{.gap}
- Age 45 sits comfortably inside the range this model was fitted on, 18 to 85 years, so the data support this answer

## Try it: predict at age 150

```{r}
#| label: tryit-predict-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = c('Intercept, mmol/L', 'Slope, mmol/L per year', 'Observed age range, years'),
  Value = c(round(int_age$estimate, 3), round(slope_age$estimate, 5), '18 to 85')
) |>
  gt()
```

- Work out the predicted mean cholesterol for a person aged 150
- Do you believe the answer, and what in the model would have warned you?[]{.gap}
- Three minutes

## Try it: the answer

- `r round(int_age$estimate, 3)` plus `r round(slope_age$estimate, 5)` times 150 gives `r round(pred_age[2, 'fit'], 2)` mmol/L, with a CI for the mean of `r round(pred_age[2, 'lwr'], 2)` to `r round(pred_age[2, 'upr'], 2)` mmol/L[]{.gap}
- That's an entirely ordinary cholesterol reading, next to a narrow CI. Nothing in the output looks wrong
- The model holds no information about anyone over 85, and answers anyway
- The only check is the one we make, on the input, against the range the model was fitted on

## Gentamicin clearance in babies: how much per kilogram? {.smaller}

| Quantity | Estimate | 95% CI | p |
|----------|----|--------|---|
| Intercept, l/h | -0.027 | -0.047 to -0.008 | 0.008 |
| Slope, per kg of weight, l/h | 0.074 | 0.066 to 0.082 | < 0.001 |

- Gentamicin is an antibiotic given for serious infections in newborns, and the kidneys clear it, so the safe dose depends on the baby's clearance[]{.gap}
- Gentamicin clearance (l/h) regressed on weight (kg), `r gent_n` babies. R squared `r gent_r2`[]{.gap}
- Clearance was on average `r gent_slope` l/h higher per additional kg of weight (95% CI `r gent_slope_ci[1]` to `r gent_slope_ci[2]` l/h, p < 0.001)[]{.gap}
- For a 3 kg baby, the predicted clearance is `r gent_pred_3kg` l/h, and the dose follows from it

## A 300 g baby: an impossible prediction

- What about a very preterm baby born at 25 weeks, weighing only 300 g?
- The same formula for a 300 g baby returns a clearance of `r gent_pred_300g` l/h
- A negative clearance is physically impossible[]{.gap}
- The linear regression model assumes the response changes *linearly* with the explanatory variable
- 300 g is also far below the lightest baby in the data, about 0.9 kg: an extrapolation

## Is sedentary time associated with cholesterol? {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lm-sed-table
#| echo: false
tibble(
  Quantity = 'Slope, cholesterol per hour/day of sedentary time, mmol/L',
  Estimate = round(slope_sed$estimate, 4),
  `95% CI` = paste0(round(slope_sed$conf.low, 4), ' to ', round(slope_sed$conf.high, 4)),
  p = format(round(slope_sed$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3)
) |>
  gt()
```
- Each additional hour/day of sedentary time was associated with a difference in cholesterol of `r round(slope_sed$estimate, 4)` mmol/L (95% CI `r round(slope_sed$conf.low, 4)` to `r round(slope_sed$conf.high, 4)` mmol/L, p = `r format(round(slope_sed$p.value, 3), nsmall = 3)`)
- The slope is close to zero, and small next to its own 95% CI[]{.gap}
- The CI includes zero, so these data are consistent with no association. R squared is essentially zero
- Cholesterol varies with age, and sedentary time might too
- Is age a confounder? Can we deal with it in the regression model?
- Next week answers that question

## Application {background-image="assets/skyline.jpg" background-size="cover" .divider}

## Two numbers, no interpretation {.smaller}

| Quantity | Estimate | 95% CI | p |
|----------|----|--------|---|
| BMI, per additional hour/day of sleep, kg/m² | -0.46 | -0.69 to -0.24 | < 0.001 |

- Potter, Cade, and Hardie (2017), *PLOS ONE*: [sleep duration and BMI in `r format(app_n, big.mark = ',')` UK adults](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0182195), adjusted for age, ethnicity, sex, smoking, and socioeconomic status[]{.gap}
- In pairs: write one sentence interpreting this coefficient in context and in its units, and one sentence stating what the model assumes
- Five minutes

## The sentences, and what the authors wrote

- BMI was on average 0.46 kg/m² lower for each additional hour/day of sleep (95% CI 0.24 to 0.69 kg/m² lower, p < 0.001), after adjustment for age, ethnicity, sex, smoking, and socioeconomic status[]{.gap}
- The model assumes linearity, constant variance, normally distributed residuals, and independence between participants
- The authors' own sentence: 'participants had 0.46 kg/m2 lower BMI values (95% CI -0.69 to -0.24 kg/m2, p < 0.001) per additional hour of sleep'
- Also an accurate description

## Key points, and what the lab does {.smaller}

- A correlation coefficient says how strongly two continuous variables move together, but not by what amount
- A regression slope quantifies the amount, in the units of the response per unit of the explanatory variable, with a CI and a p-value[]{.gap}
- Which variable is the response is an epidemiological assumption, not a statistical question
- A regression model is only valid if assumptions are reasonably met, and prediction is only reliable if we avoid extrapolation
